items.title: Why Your Phone Wins Before You Decide
items.proposed_action_to_validate: Move the phone out of sight
items.description:
Ever unlock your phone and wonder what you meant to check?

Stiles explores the checking habit: brief, repeated looks at a phone, sometimes triggered by a quiet moment. New information can reinforce another check. For your next work block, try putting the phone out of sight and out of reach. This is a small experiment, not a cure or a guarantee.

items.description:
A tiny conversational pause can feel awkward without proving rejection. A crossed-out price is a starting point, not proof of value. In a classic anchoring demonstration, arbitrary wheel numbers influenced later estimates about the United Nations. items.title: Before You Switch Tasks, Leave a Way Back
items.proposed_action_to_validate: Write a brief return plan before switching tasks
items.description:
You can leave a report without leaving it behind in your attention.

Stiles explores attention residue and a practical restart note: where you stopped, the next concrete step, and when you plan to return. The report/meeting note shown is an illustrative example, not the study's verbatim instructions.

Leroy & Glomb (2018) investigated anticipated time pressure on resuming interrupted work, attention residue, and performance on the interrupting task. A brief ready-to-resume plan mitigated these effects. This is not a claim that switching becomes cost-free, a guaranteed productivity gain, or proof of faster resumption in every setting.

Research:
https://doi.org/10.1287/orsc.2017.1184
University repository / original article abstract:
https://experts.umn.edu/en/publications/tasks-interrupted-how-anticipating-time-pressure-on-resumption-of/
Reporting and author interview (same study, not an independent replication):
https://mndaily.com/city/adproductivity/01/29/2018/snoadmin/

items.title: Why Familiar Claims Feel True
items.proposed_action_to_validate: Check evidence rather than repetition
items.description:
Hearing it again is not the same as getting new evidence.

Stiles explores the illusory truth effect: repeated statements can feel more truthful, even when people possess relevant contradictory knowledge. This does not mean knowledge is useless, every repetition persuades everyone, or every familiar claim is false.

The three-posts/one-source diagram is a conceptual example, not study data. Tracing original evidence and looking for genuinely independent reliable support are practical media-literacy suggestions, not a guaranteed cure tested by these studies.

Sources:
Fazio, Brashier, Payne & Marsh (2015), Knowledge Does Not Protect Against Illusory Truth.
https://www.apa.org/pubs/journals/features/xge-0000098.pdf
Fazio (2020), Repetition Increases Perceived Truth Even for Known Falsehoods. This follow-up measured prior knowledge before the repetition manipulation.
https://doi.org/10.1525/collabra.347
https://online.ucpress.edu/collabra/article/6/1/38/114468/Repetition-Increases-Perceived-Truth-Even-for

After a conversation, your guess about their opinion may be harsher than their actual report. Stiles explores the liking gap, one possible explanation and the difference between an observation and an interpretation.

items.title: Same Money, Different Story
items.mechanism_to_research: Reference-dependent framing of equivalent final prospects
items.proposed_action_to_validate: Compare the same choice in gains and losses
items.description:
The same final money can look different when framed as a gain or a loss. Stiles explains reference dependence, equivalent sure/gamble choices and a practical comparison checklist.

Kahneman & Tversky (1979), Prospect Theory, Problems11–12. Hypothetical between-group choices, original Israeli pounds; this video illustrates generic money units, not a real-dollar experiment or same-person reversal. Both sure outcomes1500; both gambles50%1000/50%2000. Barberis review provides context, not an independent replication.
https://doi.org/10.2307/1914185
https://www.nber.org/papers/w18621

No universal twice-as-painful claim. Final amounts/probabilities/real costs checklist is practical advice, not a tested intervention. AI-generated illustrations, opening animation and voice; authored UI and original procedural SFX, NOT Fish-generated sound effects. No music.
